G-200.statement: A grid has '1' for land and '0' for water. Land cells touching up, down, left or right form one island. Count the islands.
G-200.follow_up: Now land is added one cell at a time. Can you give the island count after each add?
G-200.key_insight: Each island is one connected group. Flood fill (spread to all touching land) marks the whole island. So you count it once.

G-207.statement: You have courses and pairs like 'take A before B'. Can you finish all the courses?
G-207.follow_up: Return the smallest number of terms (semesters) needed to finish everything.
G-207.key_insight: You can finish all courses only if the 'before' links never form a loop (a cycle).

G-994.statement: A grid has empty cells, fresh oranges and rotten oranges. Each minute, rot spreads to touching fresh oranges. Return the minutes until none are fresh, or -1.
G-994.follow_up: What if rot spreads at a different speed in each cell?
G-994.key_insight: Start BFS (visit level by level) from all rotten oranges together. Each level is one minute.

G-547.statement: You get an n x n table showing which cities are directly linked. Count the groups of cities that are linked together.
G-547.follow_up: What if links between cities are added and removed over time?
G-547.key_insight: Each group is a connected component. With union-find (merge groups), every merge of two separate groups lowers the count by one.

G-133.statement: You get one node of a connected graph with two-way edges. Return a full new copy of the whole graph.
G-133.follow_up: The graph is split across many machines by node id. How do you copy it?
G-133.key_insight: Keep a map from each old node to its copy. Save the copy before visiting neighbours, so loops reuse it.

G-210.statement: You have courses and 'take A before B' pairs. Return one order to take all courses, or an empty list if impossible.
G-210.follow_up: What if the 'before' rules change often?
G-210.key_insight: Topological sort (order by dependencies): keep taking a course with no rules left. The order you take them is a valid answer.

G-127.statement: Change the start word into the end word, one letter at a time. Every middle word must be in the list. Return the fewest words in the chain.
G-127.follow_up: Searching from both ends at once is faster. Why?
G-127.key_insight: Words are nodes; one-letter changes are edges. BFS (visit level by level) finds fewest steps. Group words by patterns like h*t to find neighbours fast.

G-269.statement: Some words are sorted using an unknown alphabet. Find a letter order that fits this sorting.
G-269.follow_up: Return all possible letter orders, or check if only one order is possible.
G-269.key_insight: Two neighbouring words only teach one rule: their first different letter. A topological sort (order by rules) of these rules gives the alphabet.

G-743.statement: A signal starts at node k and travels along timed one-way edges. When do all nodes get it? Return -1 if some never do.
G-743.follow_up: What if some edge times can be negative?
G-743.key_insight: Find the shortest time to every node with Dijkstra (always expand the closest node). The answer is the biggest of these times.

G-721.statement: Each account has a name and some emails. Merge accounts that share at least one email.
G-721.follow_up: What if the accounts are stored in different data centres?
G-721.key_insight: Emails are the links. With union-find (merge groups), join all emails of one account. Each final group is one person.

G-329.statement: You get a grid of numbers. Move up, down, left or right, always to a bigger number. Find the longest such path.
G-329.follow_up: Return the path itself. Can you solve it without recursion?
G-329.key_insight: Moves only go to bigger numbers, so loops are impossible. Compute each cell's best path once and save it (memoisation).

G-310.statement: You get a tree with n nodes as a list of edges. Return every node that gives the shortest tree height when used as the root.
G-310.follow_up: Edges are added one at a time. Keep the answer updated without starting again.
G-310.key_insight: The best roots are the tree's middle nodes. Remove all leaves, layer by layer, until only 1 or 2 nodes remain.

G-1631.statement: A grid has a height in each cell. Go from top-left to bottom-right. Make the biggest height jump between neighbouring path cells as small as possible.
G-1631.follow_up: The grid is huge and stored in pieces on disk. How do you search it?
G-1631.key_insight: Path cost is its biggest jump, and it never gets smaller as the path grows. So Dijkstra (always expand the cheapest cell) still works.

G-417.statement: Water flows to touching cells of equal or lower height. Pacific touches top and left edges, Atlantic bottom and right. Return cells that reach both oceans.
G-417.follow_up: Heights keep changing from sensors. Keep the answer correct without full recomputing.
G-417.key_insight: Think backwards: from each ocean's border, spread uphill to equal or higher cells. Cells reached from both oceans are the answer.

G-827.statement: You get an n x n grid of 0s and 1s. You may change at most one 0 into 1. Return the biggest island size possible.
G-827.follow_up: Now you may change up to K cells.
G-827.key_insight: Give each island an id and record its size once. For each 0, add 1 to the sizes of its different touching islands.

G-444.statement: You get an ordering of numbers and some short ordered lists. Is that ordering the only shortest one that keeps every list's order?
G-444.follow_up: Lists arrive one by one as logs. Find the moment the order becomes the only one.
G-444.key_insight: Use Kahn's algorithm (keep taking items with no rules left). The order is unique only if one item is ready each time.

G-787.statement: Flights have prices. Find the cheapest price from src to dst using at most k stops in between. Return -1 if impossible.
G-787.follow_up: Why does plain Dijkstra fail when there is a stop limit?
G-787.key_insight: Do at most k + 1 rounds of price updates (Bellman-Ford). Copy prices each round, so no route uses extra flights.

G-399.statement: You get equations like a / b = 2.0. Answer questions like a / c, or -1.0 if unknown.
G-399.follow_up: Answer a million questions fast. Hint: weighted union-find (merge groups with ratios).
G-399.key_insight: a / b = 2 gives edge a -> b with weight 2. It also gives b -> a with weight 1/2. A question is the product of weights on a path.

G-815.statement: Each bus drives in a loop through a list of stops. Find the fewest buses to go from source stop to target stop, or -1.
G-815.follow_up: What if you must minimise total travel time, with a cost for each bus change?
G-815.key_insight: Search over buses, not stops. Each BFS level (visit level by level) means taking one more bus.

G-778.statement: An n x n grid has different heights. Water rises by one each second. Find the earliest time you can swim from top-left to bottom-right.
G-778.follow_up: Answer the earliest time for 100,000 different start and end pairs.
G-778.key_insight: Find a path whose highest cell is as low as possible. Use Dijkstra with max(), or add cells by height until start and end connect.

G-2045.statement: Each road takes `time` minutes. Each node's light changes green and red every `change` minutes; leave only on green. Return the second smallest time from node 1 to n.
G-2045.follow_up: Now roads take different times. What replaces BFS?
G-2045.key_insight: All roads take equal time. BFS (visit level by level) finds the second smallest road count, keeping two visits per node. Then add light waits.

G-332.statement: You get plane tickets as [from, to]. Build a trip from JFK using every ticket once. If many work, return the alphabetically smallest.
G-332.follow_up: Ten million tickets are stored in many data centres. How do you check the trip?
G-332.key_insight: Using every edge once is an Eulerian path. DFS (go deep first) to the smallest place first, add airports when going back, then reverse.

G-126.statement: Change the start word into the end word, one letter at a time. Use only list words. Return all shortest chains.
G-126.follow_up: There are too many shortest chains. Produce them one by one instead of all at once.
G-126.key_insight: BFS (visit level by level) keeps only parent links on shortest paths. Walk back from the end through them to list all chains.

G-1192.statement: Servers form a network with two-way links. Return every link whose removal stops some servers from reaching others.
G-1192.follow_up: Links break and come back in real time. Keep the list of critical links updated.
G-1192.key_insight: Use Tarjan's DFS with visit times. A link is critical if, without it, the child cannot reach back up: low[child] > disc[parent].

G-305.statement: A grid starts as all water. Cells become land one at a time. After each change, return the number of islands.
G-305.follow_up: Cells can also become water again. Why does union-find fail, and what replaces it?
G-305.key_insight: Union-find (merge groups): each new land cell adds one island. Each merge with a touching island removes one.

G-2812.statement: Some cells of an n x n grid hold thieves. A path's safety is its smallest distance to any thief. Find the safest path from top-left to bottom-right.
G-2812.follow_up: Thieves move every second. Update the safest path without starting again.
G-2812.key_insight: First, BFS (visit level by level) from all thieves gives each cell's distance. Then find a path whose smallest distance is largest.

G-236.statement: In a binary tree, find the lowest common ancestor of two nodes. That is the deepest node with both below it or equal to it.
G-236.follow_up: What if nodes know their parent? What if one node may be missing?
G-236.key_insight: Use post-order (children first). Answer: the first node with a target on each side, or that is a target.

G-98.statement: Check if a binary tree is a valid binary search tree. Left side values must be smaller, right side values bigger.
G-98.follow_up: Do it without recursion and with almost no extra memory (Morris traversal).
G-98.key_insight: Each node must fit in a (low, high) range. All ancestors set this range, not only the parent.

G-199.statement: Look at a binary tree from its right side. Return the values you can see, from top to bottom.
G-199.follow_up: Return both the left view and the right view in one pass.
G-199.key_insight: The visible node is the last one on each level of BFS (visit level by level).

G-230.statement: Return the k-th smallest value in a binary search tree (smaller values left, bigger right).
G-230.follow_up: What if the tree changes often and you ask often?
G-230.key_insight: In-order traversal (left, node, right) of a search tree gives sorted values. Stop at the k-th one.

G-543.statement: Return the length of the longest path between any two nodes of a binary tree. Count the edges.
G-543.follow_up: Solve the same problem when nodes can have many children.
G-543.key_insight: The longest path through a node is left height plus right height. Take the biggest over all nodes.

G-208.statement: Build a prefix tree with three functions. Insert a word, and search for a full word. Also check if any word starts with a prefix.
G-208.follow_up: Add delete. Also make the tree smaller by joining single-child chains (radix tree).
G-208.key_insight: Words with the same start share nodes. So each action costs the word's length, not the number of words.

G-103.statement: Return a binary tree's values level by level. Go left-to-right on one level, then right-to-left on the next, and so on.
G-103.follow_up: Send each level as soon as it is done, using memory for one level only.
G-103.key_insight: It is normal BFS (visit level by level). Only reverse the output direction on every other level.

G-297.statement: Write two functions. One turns a binary tree into a string. The other turns that string back into the same tree.
G-297.follow_up: How can you make the string short for an almost full tree?
G-297.key_insight: Pre-order (node, then left, then right) with markers for empty children fixes the shape. One pass rebuilds the tree.

G-124.statement: Each binary tree node has a number, maybe negative. Find the biggest sum of any path between two nodes.
G-124.follow_up: Return the path itself, not just the sum.
G-124.key_insight: Return to the parent the best single downward branch, dropping negatives. Update the global best with left + node + right.

G-105.statement: You get a tree's pre-order list (node, left, right) and in-order list (left, node, right). Rebuild the binary tree.
G-105.follow_up: Why can pre-order and post-order lists not rebuild one unique tree?
G-105.key_insight: The first pre-order value is the root. Its place in the in-order list splits left and right subtrees.

G-863.statement: You get a binary tree and a target node. Return all nodes exactly k edges away from it.
G-863.follow_up: Answer many target and k questions quickly.
G-863.key_insight: Add a parent link to each node, so the tree becomes a normal graph. Then BFS (visit level by level) k steps.

G-212.statement: A board has letters, and you have a list of words. Find all words you can spell using touching cells, each cell once.
G-212.follow_up: What if there are a million words and the board is huge?
G-212.key_insight: Put all words in a trie (prefix tree). One DFS (go deep first) on the board checks all words and stops on dead prefixes.

G-1483.statement: A tree is given as parent[i] for each node. Build getKthAncestor(node, k): go up k parents and return that node, or -1.
G-1483.follow_up: Reuse the jump table to find lowest common ancestors in O(log N) time.
G-1483.key_insight: Binary lifting (jumps by powers of two): store each node's 1st, 2nd, 4th... ancestor. Make one jump per 1 bit of k.

G-987.statement: Group a binary tree's values by column, left to right. Inside a column, sort by row, then by value.
G-987.follow_up: How can you avoid sorting everything at the end?
G-987.key_insight: Save (column, row, value) for every node, then sort. Nodes in the same spot are sorted by value.

G-642.statement: A user types a sentence letter by letter. After each letter, return the 3 most used old sentences with that start. '#' ends and saves the sentence.
G-642.follow_up: Serve 100,000 requests per second worldwide. What can be cached, and how old may it be?
G-642.key_insight: Use a trie (prefix tree) with sentence counts. Each typed letter moves one node deeper and returns that node's top 3.

G-23.statement: You get k sorted linked lists. Merge them into one sorted list.
G-23.follow_up: Each list is on another machine, and you have only 64MB of memory.
G-23.key_insight: Only the front of each list can be next. A heap (fast smallest-item box) of k fronts finds it in O(log k).

G-347.statement: You get a list of numbers. Return the k numbers that appear most often.
G-347.follow_up: What if the input is a stream of a billion events?
G-347.key_insight: Count each number. Keep a size-k min-heap (smallest on top). The least common of the top k leaves first.

G-215.statement: Return the k-th largest number in an unsorted list.
G-215.follow_up: Quickselect is fast on average but slow in the worst case. How do you protect it?
G-215.key_insight: A size-k min-heap (smallest on top) keeps the k largest numbers seen. Its top is the k-th largest.

G-1094.statement: A car has a seat limit and only drives east. Each trip is [people, from, to]. Can it do all trips without going over the limit?
G-1094.follow_up: What if places go up to a billion and trips arrive as a stream?
G-1094.key_insight: The load only changes at pick-ups and drop-offs. Go through these events in order and check the running total.

G-295.statement: Build a tool that adds numbers one by one. At any time, it must return the median (middle value).
G-295.follow_up: What if 99% of numbers are between 0 and 100?
G-295.key_insight: Use two heaps (fast top-item boxes). A max-heap holds the small half; a min-heap holds the big half. Keep sizes within one.

G-621.statement: Run tasks, one per time unit. Two same tasks need n time units between them. Find the least total time.
G-621.follow_up: Return the real schedule, not just its length.
G-621.key_insight: The most frequent task sets the frame. Answer: (maxFreq - 1) * (n + 1) + tasks tied at maxFreq, or the task count if bigger.

G-1834.statement: Each task has a start time and a run time. One CPU always runs the shortest waiting task, ties by index. Return the run order.
G-1834.follow_up: Now there are K CPUs, and tasks have priorities. What changes?
G-1834.key_insight: Simulate the clock with a min-heap (smallest on top). Add tasks that arrived, run the shortest, and jump ahead if nothing waits.

G-56.statement: You get a list of time ranges [start, end]. Join all ranges that overlap and return the result.
G-56.follow_up: Ranges arrive one by one. Keep the joined set updated.
G-56.key_insight: Sort by start. Then a range can only overlap the last joined one, so one pass joins everything.

G-57.statement: You get sorted ranges that do not overlap. Add a new range, joining ranges that overlap it.
G-57.follow_up: The list is huge. Use binary search to do it faster.
G-57.key_insight: Ranges ending before the new one stay. Overlapping ones join into it. The rest come after.

G-253.statement: You get meeting times as [start, end]. Find the smallest number of rooms needed for all meetings.
G-253.follow_up: Also return which room each meeting uses.
G-253.key_insight: Rooms needed equals the most meetings at the same moment. Go through starts and ends in time order (sweep line).

G-759.statement: Each worker has a sorted list of busy times. Return the free times that all workers share, ignoring the open ends.
G-759.follow_up: What if schedules are in different time zones and systems?
G-759.key_insight: Join everyone's busy times into one sorted timeline. The gaps between them are the shared free time.

G-1235.statement: Each job has a start, end and profit. Choose jobs that do not overlap to get the biggest total profit.
G-1235.follow_up: What if you have K machines instead of one?
G-1235.key_insight: Sort by end time. Best = max(skip this job, take it + best before its start). Find that earlier job with binary search.

G-2402.statement: There are n rooms, 0 to n-1. Each meeting takes the lowest free room. If none is free, it waits and keeps its length. Return the busiest room.
G-2402.follow_up: What if rooms have different sizes and meetings have different group sizes?
G-2402.key_insight: Use two min-heaps (smallest on top): free rooms by number, busy rooms by (end time, number). A waiting meeting takes the first room to free.

G-198.statement: Houses in a row hold money. You cannot rob two houses next to each other. Find the most money you can rob.
G-198.follow_up: What if the houses are in a circle, or in a tree?
G-198.key_insight: best[i] = max(best[i - 1], best[i - 2] + money[i]). Either skip this house or rob it.

G-62.statement: In a grid, go from top-left to bottom-right, moving only right or down. Count the different paths.
G-62.follow_up: Add blocked cells. What if the grid is 100,000 by 100,000?
G-62.key_insight: Paths into a cell = paths from above + paths from the left.

G-91.statement: Letters are coded as numbers: 'A'=1 up to 'Z'=26. Count how many ways a digit string can be decoded.
G-91.follow_up: Add a '*' digit that can mean any digit from 1 to 9.
G-91.key_insight: Add ways[i - 1] if the last digit is valid. Add ways[i - 2] if the last two digits are 10 to 26.

G-139.statement: You get a string and a list of words. Can you cut the string into words from the list?
G-139.follow_up: Return all possible sentences. What grows too large?
G-139.key_insight: DP (save small answers): ok[i] is true if a list word ends at i. Also ok must be true where that word starts.

G-5.statement: A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards. Return the longest palindrome made of next-to-each-other letters in s.
G-5.follow_up: How does Manacher's algorithm make this O(N)?
G-5.key_insight: Every palindrome mirrors around a centre. Grow outwards from each of the 2n - 1 centres to check them all.

G-416.statement: Can you split a list of numbers into two groups with equal sums?
G-416.follow_up: Split into K groups with equal sums instead.
G-416.key_insight: It is subset sum to half the total. Track which sums you can reach, using each number only once.

G-152.statement: A subarray is a run of items next to each other. Find the subarray with the biggest product.
G-152.follow_up: Return the subarray itself. Handle products too big for 64 bits.
G-152.key_insight: A negative number can turn the smallest product into the biggest. So track both max and min product ending here.

G-322.statement: You get coin values and an amount. Find the fewest coins that add up to the amount, or -1.
G-322.follow_up: Count the number of ways instead. Which loop goes outside?
G-322.key_insight: DP (save small answers). Fewest coins for amount a = 1 + the min over coins of fewest coins for a - coin.

G-300.statement: Pick items from a list in order, skipping any you like. Find the longest picked sequence where each item is bigger.
G-300.follow_up: Rebuild one longest sequence. Also count all longest sequences.
G-300.key_insight: Keep the smallest possible last value for each length. Use binary search to find where each number goes.

G-1143.statement: A subsequence keeps letters in order but may skip some. Return the length of the longest one shared by two strings.
G-1143.follow_up: Compare two 1GB files. What must change (Hirschberg or Myers)?
G-1143.key_insight: DP table (save small answers): if last letters match, extend the answer for both shorter parts. Otherwise drop one letter from either side.

G-72.statement: Turn one word into another using insert, delete or replace of one letter. Find the fewest steps.
G-72.follow_up: Return the actual list of edit steps.
G-72.key_insight: DP table (save small answers). Each cell takes the cheapest of insert, delete or replace on shorter word starts.

G-410.statement: Split a list into k non-empty parts of items next to each other. Make the biggest part sum as small as possible.
G-410.follow_up: The list is a stream of a billion numbers. Find a near-best split with little memory.
G-410.key_insight: If max part sum S works, any bigger S works too. Binary search S, and greedily count the parts needed.

G-42.statement: Bars of given heights stand in a row. After rain, how much water is held between them?
G-42.follow_up: Solve the 2D version, where heights form a grid.
G-42.key_insight: Water above a bar = min(tallest bar left, tallest bar right) - its height. Prefix maximums or two pointers find this.

G-10.statement: Match a whole string with a pattern. '.' matches any one letter. '*' means zero or more of the letter before it.
G-10.follow_up: Add '+' (one or more) and '?' (zero or one).
G-10.key_insight: DP (save small answers). x* can match nothing and be skipped. Or it eats one letter and stays.

G-312.statement: Burst balloons one by one. Bursting i gives nums[left] * nums[i] * nums[right], using its current neighbours. Find the most coins.
G-312.follow_up: Why does choosing the first balloon to burst not work?
G-312.key_insight: Interval DP: pick the balloon burst last in a range. Its neighbours are then the range edges, so both halves are separate.

G-739.statement: For each day, return how many days until a warmer day. Use 0 if no warmer day comes.
G-739.follow_up: The data is a live feed, and answers may come late. What changes?
G-739.key_insight: Keep waiting days on a stack with falling temperatures. A warmer day answers every colder day on top.

G-503.statement: The list is circular: after the end, it starts again. For each item, return the next bigger item, or -1.
G-503.follow_up: Values keep coming forever. Output each answer as soon as it is known.
G-503.key_insight: Use a monotonic stack (stack kept in sorted order). For the circle, go over the indices twice using i mod n.

G-84.statement: Bars of a chart have given heights and width 1. Find the area of the biggest rectangle inside the bars.
G-84.follow_up: How can this help find the biggest rectangle of 1s in a 0/1 grid?
G-84.key_insight: A bar's widest rectangle reaches the nearest shorter bar on each side. Find these when popping from a rising stack.

G-239.statement: A window of size k slides over a list, one step at a time. Return the biggest value in each window.
G-239.follow_up: What if you also need each window's median?
G-239.key_insight: Use a deque (two-ended queue) with falling values. Drop values that can never be the max again. The front is the max.

G-862.statement: Find the shortest run of items next to each other with sum at least k. Return -1 if none. Numbers can be negative.
G-862.follow_up: Answer it for 100,000 different values of k.
G-862.key_insight: Use prefix sums and a deque (two-ended queue) of rising sums. Pop front while sum reaches k; pop back if a smaller sum arrives.

G-1944.statement: People stand in a line with different heights. For each person, count people on their right they can see. Everyone between must be shorter than both.
G-1944.follow_up: People join and leave the line. Answer the questions quickly.
G-1944.key_insight: Go right to left with a falling stack. Each person sees everyone shorter they pop, plus the next taller person if any.

R-200.prompt: A grid has '1' for land and '0' for water. Touching land cells (up, down, left, right) make one island. Count the islands.
R-200.pattern: DFS or BFS flood fill: from each new land cell, spread to all touching land and mark it.

R-207.prompt: You have courses and 'take A before B' pairs. Can you finish all the courses?
R-207.pattern: Find a loop (cycle): Kahn's algorithm (take items with no rules left) or DFS (go deep first) with 3 colours.
R-207.edge_case: A course that needs itself first.

R-994.prompt: A grid has fresh and rotten oranges. Each minute rot spreads to touching fresh ones. Return minutes until none are fresh, or -1.
R-994.pattern: Multi-source BFS (visit level by level from many starts): start from all rotten oranges at once.
R-994.edge_case: No fresh oranges at the start: return 0.

R-547.prompt: You get an n x n table of which cities are directly linked. Count the groups of linked cities.
R-547.pattern: Union-find (merge groups of items), or DFS (go deep first), over the table.
R-547.edge_case: Each city is linked to itself on the diagonal.

R-133.prompt: You get one node of a connected graph with two-way edges. Return a full new copy of the graph.
R-133.pattern: DFS or BFS (walk the graph) with a hash map from each old node to its copy.
R-133.edge_case: Loops: reuse the existing copy, or you recurse forever.

R-210.prompt: You have courses and 'take A before B' pairs. Return one order to take all of them, or an empty list.
R-210.pattern: Topological sort (order by dependencies) using Kahn's algorithm: keep taking courses with no rules left.
R-210.edge_case: A loop exists if the result has fewer courses than the total.

R-127.prompt: Change the start word into the end word, one letter at a time. Use only list words. Return the fewest words in the chain.
R-127.pattern: BFS (visit level by level), finding neighbour words through pattern groups like h*t.
R-127.edge_case: The end word is not in the list.

R-269.prompt: Some words are sorted using an unknown alphabet. Find a letter order that fits this sorting.
R-269.pattern: Get rules from neighbouring words, then topological sort (order by the rules).
R-269.edge_case: A longer word before its own prefix, like ['abc', 'ab'], is invalid.

R-743.prompt: A signal starts at node k and travels along timed one-way edges. When do all nodes get it? Return -1 if never.
R-743.pattern: Dijkstra (always expand the closest node) with a min-heap (smallest on top).
R-743.edge_case: Some nodes can never be reached.

R-721.prompt: Each account has a name and some emails. Merge accounts that share at least one email.
R-721.pattern: Union-find (merge groups of items) on the emails.
R-721.edge_case: The same name does not mean the same person.

R-329.prompt: In a grid of numbers, move up, down, left or right, always to a bigger number. Find the longest such path.
R-329.pattern: DFS (go deep first) plus memoisation (save each cell's answer). Paths cannot loop, so it is a DAG.
R-329.edge_case: Equal neighbours do not count as bigger.

R-310.prompt: You get a tree as a list of edges. Return every node that gives the smallest tree height when used as root.
R-310.pattern: Topological peeling (remove leaves layer by layer) until 1 or 2 nodes are left.

R-1631.prompt: A grid has heights. Go from top-left to bottom-right. Make the biggest height jump between neighbouring path cells as small as possible.
R-1631.pattern: Dijkstra (always expand the cheapest cell) with a min-heap. Path cost is the biggest jump so far.

R-417.prompt: Water flows to touching cells of equal or lower height. Pacific is top/left, Atlantic bottom/right. Return cells reaching both.
R-417.pattern: Reverse flood fill: from each ocean's border, spread uphill to equal or higher cells.
R-417.edge_case: Border cells already touch an ocean.

R-236.prompt: In a binary tree, find the lowest common ancestor of two nodes. That is the deepest node with both below it.
R-236.pattern: Post-order DFS (children before parent): each subtree returns the target node it found.
R-236.edge_case: One node is an ancestor of the other.

R-98.prompt: Check if a binary tree is a valid binary search tree. Left values must be smaller, right values bigger.
R-98.pattern: DFS (go deep first) passing (low, high) limits down, or check that in-order gives sorted values.

R-199.prompt: Look at a binary tree from its right side. Return the values you can see, top to bottom.
R-199.pattern: BFS (visit level by level), and take the last node of each level.
R-199.edge_case: The left subtree is deeper than the right one.

R-230.prompt: Return the k-th smallest value in a binary search tree.
R-230.pattern: In-order traversal (left, node, right) with a counter, which visits values in sorted order.
R-230.edge_case: k equals the number of nodes.

R-543.prompt: Find the longest path between any two nodes of a binary tree. Return its length in edges.
R-543.pattern: DFS (go deep first) returns heights; update a global best with left + right.
R-543.edge_case: The longest path may not pass through the root.

R-208.prompt: Build a prefix tree with insert, search for a full word, and startsWith for a prefix.
R-208.pattern: Trie nodes (one node per letter step), each with a children map and an end-of-word flag.
R-208.edge_case: A prefix that is also a full word.

R-103.prompt: Return a binary tree's values level by level. Switch direction on each level: left-to-right, then right-to-left.
R-103.pattern: BFS (visit level by level); reverse every other level, or fill a deque from alternating ends.

R-297.prompt: Write two functions. One turns a binary tree into a string. The other turns it back.
R-297.pattern: Pre-order (node, left, right) with markers for empty children.
R-297.edge_case: Negative values and values with many digits.

R-23.prompt: You get k sorted linked lists. Merge them into one sorted list.
R-23.pattern: Min-heap (fast smallest-item box) holding the front node of each list.

R-347.prompt: You get a list of numbers. Return the k numbers that appear most often.
R-347.pattern: Count each number, then keep a size-k min-heap (smallest on top). Bucket sort by count also works.

R-215.prompt: Return the k-th largest number in an unsorted list.
R-215.pattern: Size-k min-heap (smallest on top), or quickselect (partial quicksort).

R-1094.prompt: A car has a seat limit and only drives east. Trips are [people, from, to]. Can it do all trips without going over?
R-1094.pattern: Sort by pick-up plus a min-heap (smallest on top) of drop-offs. Or a difference array (add/subtract at points).
R-1094.edge_case: At the same place, drop people off before picking new ones up.

R-56.prompt: You get time ranges [start, end]. Join all ranges that overlap and return the result.
R-56.pattern: Sort by start, then join each range into the last one if they overlap.
R-56.edge_case: Touching ranges like [1,4] and [4,5] should join.

R-57.prompt: You get sorted ranges that do not overlap. Add a new range, joining any it overlaps.
R-57.pattern: Three-part scan: ranges before it, ranges overlapping it, ranges after it.
R-57.edge_case: The new range comes before all, or after all, existing ranges.

R-253.prompt: You get meeting times [start, end]. Find the fewest rooms needed for all meetings.
R-253.pattern: Min-heap (smallest on top) of end times, or a sweep line (walk through starts and ends in time order).
R-253.edge_case: A meeting ending exactly when another starts frees its room.

R-198.prompt: Houses in a row hold money. You cannot rob two houses next to each other. Find the most money.
R-198.pattern: 1D DP (save answers for smaller rows): at each house, rob it or skip it.

R-62.prompt: In a grid, go from top-left to bottom-right moving only right or down. Count the paths.
R-62.pattern: Grid DP (each cell adds the answers from above and left), or a counting formula.
R-62.edge_case: A 1 x N grid has exactly one path.

R-91.prompt: Letters are coded 'A'=1 to 'Z'=26. Count how many ways a digit string can be decoded.
R-91.pattern: 1D DP (save answers for shorter starts), looking back one digit and two digits.

R-139.prompt: You get a string and a list of words. Can you cut the string into words from the list?
R-139.pattern: DP over prefixes (save answer for each start of the string), with the words in a set.
R-139.edge_case: The same word may be used many times.

R-5.prompt: Find the longest run of next-to-each-other letters in s. It must read the same both ways.
R-5.pattern: Grow outwards from each of the 2N - 1 centres. Interval DP (save answers for ranges) also works.
R-5.edge_case: Even-length palindromes have their centre between two letters.

R-416.prompt: Can you split a list of numbers into two groups with equal sums?
R-416.pattern: 0/1 knapsack (each item used once) over reachable sums. Loop sums downwards.

R-152.prompt: Find the run of items next to each other with the biggest product.
R-152.pattern: Track the running max and min product. A negative number swaps them.

R-322.prompt: You get coin values and an amount. Find the fewest coins that make the amount, or -1.
R-322.pattern: Unbounded knapsack (each coin used many times), finding the fewest coins.

R-739.prompt: For each day, return how many days until a warmer day. Use 0 if none comes.
R-739.pattern: Monotonic stack (stack kept in sorted order) of indices, with falling temperatures.
R-739.edge_case: Equal temperatures do not count as warmer.

R-503.prompt: The list is circular: after the end, it starts again. For each item, return the next bigger item, or -1.
R-503.pattern: Monotonic stack (stack kept in sorted order) of indices, with falling values, over two passes.

R-84.prompt: Bars of a chart have given heights and width 1. Find the area of the biggest rectangle inside the bars.
R-84.pattern: Monotonic stack (stack kept in sorted order) with rising heights, plus a sentinel (extra 0 bar at the end).
R-84.edge_case: All bars have the same height.

B-dijkstra-stale.pattern: No skip for old heap entries. Add 'if d > dist[u]: continue'. Answer stays correct, but work can grow to O(E^2) on dense graphs.
B-dijkstra-stale.edge_case: The heap holds many copies of the same node.

B-bfs-visited.pattern: BFS (visit level by level) marks a cell as seen when popped, so it is added many times. Mark it when you push it.
B-bfs-visited.edge_case: An open grid with no walls makes the queue explode.

B-union-find-root.pattern: Union-find (merge groups of items): it returns x, not the root. The last line must be `return parent[x]`.

B-bst-bounds.pattern: It only checks parent and child. A grandchild can still break the rule. Pass (low, high) limits down instead.

B-trie-prefix.prompt:
Find the bug in this trie (prefix tree) search:

  def search(self, word):
      node = self.root
      for ch in word:
          if ch not in node.children: return False
          node = node.children[ch]
      return True
B-trie-prefix.pattern: It returns True for any prefix, not only full words. The last line must be `return node.end`.
B-trie-prefix.edge_case: After insert("apple"), search("app") must be False.

B-heap-ties.prompt:
Find the bug in this merge of k sorted lists:

  heap = [(l.val, l) for l in lists if l]
  heapq.heapify(heap)
  while heap:
      val, node = heapq.heappop(heap)
      tail.next = node; tail = node
      if node.next: heapq.heappush(heap, (node.next.val, node.next))
B-heap-ties.pattern: Equal values make heapq compare ListNode objects, which gives TypeError. Push (val, unique_counter, node) instead.
B-heap-ties.edge_case: Two lists that start with the same value.

B-merge-max-end.pattern: The new end must be max(out[-1][1], e). Else [1,10] then [2,3] shrinks to [1,3]. Empty input also crashes.
B-merge-max-end.edge_case: One range lies fully inside another.

B-coin-guard.pattern: Missing the check c <= a (a negative index wraps around in Python). Also it returns inf instead of -1.
B-coin-guard.edge_case: An amount that cannot be made must return -1.

B-knapsack-direction.pattern: Going up in s lets x be used many times (unbounded knapsack). Loop s from target down to x.

B-deque-evict.pattern: It never removes indices that left the window. Add `if dq[0] <= i - k: dq.popleft()` before reading dq[0].
